title: Bitwise operators, masks, shifts and bit manipulation
learningObjectives: Distinguish bitwise AND, OR, XOR and complement from the logical operators &&, || and !.
Use unsigned integer types and bit masks to test, set, clear and toggle individual flags.
Explain integer promotions and why bitwise operations on narrow integer types may be performed after promotion to int or unsigned int.
Use left and right shifts only with valid shift counts and operands whose behaviour is well-defined for the intended operation.
Avoid assumptions about signed right shift, negative left operands, shift counts greater than or equal to the promoted operand width, and signed overflow.
Write portable flag and field-extraction code with explicit unsigned constants, parentheses and documented bit positions.
prerequisites: CL2.6 Integer types, ranges and signedness

understand.concept: Bitwise operators work on the value representation of integer operands after the language's integer promotions. AND (`&`) keeps bits set in both operands, OR (`|`) sets bits present in either operand, XOR (`^`) toggles differing bits, and complement (`~`) inverts every bit of the promoted operand. Shift operators move bits left or right by a count.
understand.whyItMatters: Bit masks are used in hardware registers, file formats, protocol flags, permissions, compact state and low-level algorithms. Incorrect signed arithmetic or invalid shift counts can produce implementation-defined behaviour or undefined behaviour.
understand.analogy: A bit mask is like a row of switches: a mask selects which switches to inspect or change.
understand.analogyLimit: C operators act on integer values after promotions, not on a visual row of independent physical switches. Type width, signedness and shift rules matter.

explain.narrative:
Use unsigned integer types for bit manipulation when you intend a logical bit pattern. To test a flag, evaluate `(flags & MASK) != 0U`. To set, use `flags |= MASK`; to clear, use `flags &= ~MASK`; to toggle, use `flags ^= MASK`. Parenthesize these expressions because bitwise operators have different precedence from comparisons and logical operators.

The right operand of a shift must be nonnegative and less than the width in bits of the promoted left operand. Left-shifting an unsigned value is reduced modulo one more than the maximum representable value; left-shifting a negative signed value or producing an unrepresentable signed result is undefined. Right shift of a negative signed value is implementation-defined. Integer promotions can change the operand type before the shift, so use explicit unsigned types and validate shift counts. Do not assume that an unsigned type is exactly 32 bits unless you have selected a type with the required width.

examples.title: Set, test, clear and toggle independent flags
examples.explanation: The flags are unsigned bit masks. OR sets bits, AND tests or clears selected bits, and XOR toggles a bit. The comparison converts the masked value to a clear Boolean-like result for printing.

examples.title: Extract a small field after validating the shift position
examples.explanation: The program checks that the shift count is smaller than the width of the unsigned int object before shifting. The mask then retains only the three selected low-order bits of the shifted value.

practise.guidedTask: Draw the low four bits of flags after each operation in the first example. Change the order of `&`, `==` and `!=` without parentheses and observe why explicit grouping improves correctness.
practise.independentTask: Define four independent unsigned flags and implement test, set, clear and toggle operations. Add a field extraction function that rejects a shift count outside the width of its operand type.
hints: Use `&` for bitwise AND and `&&` for logical AND; they are not interchangeable.
Use unsigned operands for masks and bit-pattern operations where possible.
Set with `|=`, clear with `&= ~mask`, and toggle with `^= mask`.
Check the shift count against the width of the promoted left operand before shifting.
Do not left-shift a negative signed value or assume right shift of a negative signed value is portable.
Parenthesize mask tests before comparing them; operator precedence is easy to misread.

questions.prompt: Which expression tests whether FLAG is set in flags?
questions.explanation: Bitwise AND isolates the bits present in both flags and FLAG; comparing the result with zero tests whether any selected bit is set.

questions.prompt: Which operation sets selected bits without changing other set bits?
questions.explanation: Bitwise OR sets every bit present in mask while preserving other bits already set in flags.

questions.prompt: How do you clear the bits selected by mask?
questions.explanation: Complementing the mask selects all bits outside the mask, and AND clears only the mask's selected bits.

questions.prompt: What must be true of a shift count?
options: It must be nonnegative and less than the width of the promoted left operand.
It may be any integer value.
It must always equal the width of the operand.
It must be negative for right shifts.
questions.answer: It must be nonnegative and less than the width of the promoted left operand.
questions.explanation: A shift count outside the valid range is undefined behaviour; the left operand is promoted before the shift.

questions.prompt: Which statement about right-shifting a negative signed integer is correct in C?
options: It is guaranteed to fill with zero bits.
It is always a syntax error.
questions.explanation: The C language specifies right shift of a negative signed value as implementation-defined, so portable code should avoid relying on one result.
